Fenyeslitke Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Fényeslitke, Hungary

Not demolished. Fényeslitke's Jewish cemetery appears on an 1870 cadastral map. Jewish settlement traces to 1746, when Martinus Salamonovics and his family lived in the village; by the 19th century Jews worked widely as merchants, teachers, and butchers, and owned the local distillery and mill. The Orthodox community, under the Kisvárda rabbinate, ran its own synagogue and cheder. Two Jewish soldiers, Menyhert Katz and David Weis, died fighting Russia in World War I; during the 1919 'white terror,' several Jews were taken captive to Kisvárda. Wartime forced labor took many village men to Ukraine after 1941, including Zsigmond Klein, who died in service. By April 1944 the Orthodox community numbered around 40; after Passover its members were taken to the Kisvárda Ghetto and deported to Auschwitz by the end of May, after which locals plundered the synagogue. Only a handful of survivors returned - 2 by 1946, 5 by 1949. There were no more burials in the cemetery after 1944; the last Jewish resident of Fényeslitke, Jakab Tinman, was buried in a Christian cemetery since the Jewish one had fallen into disrepair. Its tombstones were removed in the 1950s, and today only scattered fragments remain, the most recent legible one dated 1924. A Holocaust memorial listing 65 names was erected in the village in 2004.
